title: Roadmap 14: Messaging and resilience
seriesDescription: Topic-by-topic quizzes that follow the backend interview roadmap: language core, concurrency, DSA habits, web frameworks, data access, databases, messaging, resilience, security, testing, system design, and LLM/agent engineering.
description: Queues versus streams, delivery guarantees and idempotent consumers, the outbox pattern, dead-letter queues, sagas, and timeouts, retries and circuit breakers.
source: Interview roadmap study plan (Java/Spring Boot and Python/FastAPI)

questions.prompt: Several independent services each need to read the same order events, and a new service must be able to replay last week of history. Which broker model fits?

options.text: A Kafka topic: a retained log with one consumer group per service.
options.why: Right: events stay after being read and each group tracks its own offset.

options.text: A single RabbitMQ queue with all services as competing consumers.
options.why: Competing consumers split messages, so each service sees only part.

options.text: A RabbitMQ queue that deletes each message once it is acknowledged.
options.why: Acknowledged messages are removed, so nothing remains to replay.

options.text: A database table that every service polls once per second.
options.why: Possible but reinvents offsets, partitioning and retention.

questions.explanation: Queues (RabbitMQ) distribute work and remove messages once handled. Streams (Kafka) keep an ordered, replayable log that many consumer groups read independently.

questions.prompt: True or false: a broker that offers at-least-once delivery can never deliver the same message to a consumer twice.

options.text: True
options.why: At-least-once means duplicates are possible.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: after a crash or timeout before the acknowledgement, the message is redelivered.

questions.explanation: At-most-once may lose messages, at-least-once may duplicate them. True end-to-end exactly-once effects come from idempotent consumers or transactional writes.

questions.prompt: A payment-event consumer crashes after charging the customer but before committing its offset, so the event is redelivered. What prevents a double charge?

options.text: Store the event id under a unique key in the same transaction as the charge.
options.why: Right: a duplicate hits the constraint and is skipped, atomically with the effect.

options.text: Commit the offset before processing so the event can never be redelivered.
options.why: That is at-most-once: a crash after the commit loses the event.

options.text: Keep recently seen event ids in an in-memory set inside every consumer instance process.
options.why: Lost on restart and not shared between instances.

options.text: Increase the session timeout so the consumer is not considered dead.
options.why: Does not remove the window between the side effect and the commit.

questions.explanation: Assume redelivery. Use a dedup key (event id or business key) stored atomically with the effect, or make the operation naturally idempotent, for example an upsert.

questions.prompt: A service must update its database and publish an OrderCreated event, and neither may be lost. What does the outbox pattern do?

options.text: Writes the event to an outbox table in the same transaction; a relay or CDC publishes it.
options.why: Right: one local transaction, then asynchronous publishing.

options.text: Publishes to the broker first and then writes to the database in a second, separate step.
options.why: A crash between the two steps leaves them inconsistent.

options.text: Wraps the database and the broker in a two-phase commit across both systems.
options.why: Most brokers do not support it and it hurts availability.

options.text: Retries the broker publish in a catch block until the call eventually succeeds.
options.why: A crash after the commit but before the retry still loses the event.

questions.explanation: The outbox solves the dual-write problem. Debezium can tail the database log (CDC) and publish outbox rows to Kafka, giving at-least-once delivery, so consumers must be idempotent.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply. Which practices handle a poison message well?

options.text: Retry a bounded number of times with backoff, then move the message to a dead-letter queue.
options.why: Right: the main flow keeps moving.

options.text: Keep the original payload and failure reason in the DLQ and alert on its depth.
options.why: Right: someone can diagnose and replay it.

options.text: Retry instantly and forever, so ordering is preserved for later messages.
options.why: Blocks the partition or queue and burns CPU.

options.text: Drop the message silently after the first exception to keep the queue short.
options.why: Silent data loss with nothing to investigate.

options.text: Acknowledge it before processing so the broker stops redelivering it.
options.why: The message is lost if the processing then fails.

questions.explanation: Distinguish transient errors (retry) from permanent ones (DLQ at once). A DLQ without monitoring and a replay tool is just a quieter way of losing data.

questions.prompt: A booking flow has six steps across services, with branching and compensations (refund, release seat). The team wants one place to see the flow state. Which saga style fits?

options.text: Orchestration: a coordinator sends commands, tracks state and triggers compensations.
options.why: Right: explicit flow and a single place to observe and debug it.

options.text: Choreography: each service reacts to events with no central owner of the flow.
options.why: Fine for few steps, but the flow gets scattered and hard to trace here.

options.text: A distributed two-phase commit locking rows in all services until every step succeeds.
options.why: Not what a saga is; it holds locks across services.

options.text: One shared database for all services so a single transaction can cover it.
options.why: Removes service independence instead of coordinating it.

questions.explanation: Sagas replace a distributed transaction with local transactions plus compensating actions. Choreography is looser but harder to follow; orchestration centralises logic.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply. Which practices make retries safe for a downstream service?

options.text: Use exponential backoff with jitter so clients do not retry in lockstep.
options.why: Right: spreads retries over time.

options.text: Cap retries with a budget, for example a small share of recent requests.
options.why: Right: prevents a retry storm during an outage.

options.text: Retry only idempotent calls, or send an idempotency key with the request.
options.why: Right: a duplicate must not repeat the effect.

options.text: Retry at every layer of a three-tier call chain to maximise success.
options.why: Multiplies load: three layers with three attempts each means up to 27 calls.

options.text: Retry on validation errors such as HTTP 400 until the call works.
options.why: A bad request will keep failing; retry only transient failures.

questions.explanation: Every external call also needs a timeout, or one slow dependency ties up all your threads. Retries without a budget turn a partial outage into a full one.

questions.prompt: True or false: while a circuit breaker is open, calls fail fast without reaching the struggling dependency, and a half-open probe later tests whether it has recovered.

options.text: True
options.why: Correct: this gives the dependency room to recover and frees your threads.

options.text: False
options.why: It does the opposite of sending every call through.

questions.explanation: Pair it with a fallback (cached value, default, queue for later) and a bulkhead that limits how many threads or connections one dependency can use.
